title: Roses
hookLine: a dying nun makes a promise about what she'll do after she's gone

lines: A LAST WISH, BUT FOR HERSELF.
cards: A will usually tells other people what to do: who gets the house, which song to play. In the infirmary at Lisieux, Thérèse's sisters wrote down things she said in her last weeks, and one is a plan for herself. Not rest.
Work. She said she wanted to spend her heaven doing good on earth. And tradition adds an image to go with it: she would let fall a shower of roses.

teach.h: SHE PLANS TO WORK IN HEAVEN.
teach.b: First, the sentence. Her sisters kept notebooks by her bed, later gathered as her last conversations. In them she says her mission is about to begin, and that she wants to spend her heaven doing good on earth.
A strange thing for a dying nun to say: heaven, for her, sounds busy. Second, why Catholics hear it as more than a nice wish.

teach.h: THE SAINTS PRAY FOR THE LIVING.
teach.b: The Church teaches the communion of saints: those who have died in Christ aren't cut off from the living, and they pray for us. The Catechism, explaining this, quotes Thérèse's own line.
Her wish became a way the Church explains what saints do. Third, the roses.
Tradition says she spoke of letting fall a shower of roses, and people who pray to her tell of a rose turning up, a scent, a small unexpected kindness, which they take as her answer.
The Church doesn't ask anyone to read signs in flowers. Some find comfort in the custom; others pass it by. Both are at home in the Church.
Fourth, the quiet part. A falling rose doesn't announce who dropped it. The good Thérèse promised is the kind she did inside the convent walls: small, hidden, unsigned.

teach.h: LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.
teach.b: Jesus puts it this way in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Heaven doing good, and earth doing it too, without a name card.

how: Catholics ask the saints, Thérèse among them, to pray for them, and some keep a custom of asking her for a sign of roses; others simply try to do hidden good in her spirit.

o: Thérèse's sign of good done quietly from heaven
the flowers laid at her tomb on her feast day
the flowers Thérèse grew in the convent garden

p: shouldn't know what the right hand does

s: Thérèse pictured heaven mainly as a long rest
she said she wanted to spend her heaven doing good on earth.
the Catechism quotes her line about heaven
it uses her words to explain the communion of saints.
Catholics must look for roses as signs from her
it's a custom some people love and others pass by. the Church doesn't require it.

games.q: you've done something kind for a coworker, and nobody saw. at lunch someone asks who did it. what does Jesus's line about the hands suggest?
o: raise your hand so the credit lands where it belongs.
let it go unsigned: the left hand doesn't need to know.
hint that it might have been you.
games.why: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." the good Thérèse promised was like her good in the convent: small, hidden, unsigned.

practice: Look over the people you'll cross today and ask who could use something small: a coffee paid for, a dish washed before anyone asks, a kind word passed along about someone, behind their back for once.
Choose one, and choose how to keep your name off it, a rose with no card. If you pray, you can ask Thérèse to pray with you, as Catholics do; if you don't, just hold the plan steady.

wordCard.voice: Roses. Tradition's image for Thérèse's promise to spend her heaven doing good on earth: small kindnesses falling, unsigned. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven doing good. In this teaching, the saints keep praying for the living. I'll be here tomorrow.
